title: Arabic, and translation
hookLine: Muslims hold the Qur'an to be the Arabic itself, and a translation to be its meanings

lines: WHAT THE BOOK IS, AND ISN'T.
cards: Pick up an English Qur'an in a bookstore and look closely at the title page. On many copies, it doesn't simply say The Qur'an.
It says something like The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, or The Meanings of the Qur'an in English. That isn't modesty for its own sake.
It's a careful statement of what Muslims believe the book in your hands is, and what it isn't.

teach.h: THE MEANING OF THE GLORIOUS KORAN
teach.b: Muslims hold that the Qur'an is the word of God in Arabic: not only its ideas, but its actual words, sounds and order. The Qur'an says so about itself.
In Pickthall's words: "Lo! We have revealed it, a Lecture in Arabic, that ye may understand." Lecture is Pickthall's old word for a reading, a recitation; the Arabic there is qur'an.
So a translation, however good, is a human attempt to carry the meanings into another language: valuable, often essential, but Muslims don't call it the Qur'an itself.

That's why Marmaduke Pickthall, whose English you've heard all year, called his 1930 work The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, and wrote in his foreword, in effect, that the Qur'an cannot be translated and his book was only an attempt to present its meaning.

teach.h: THE PRAYER IS SAID IN ARABIC
teach.b: The ritual prayer is said in Arabic wherever a Muslim lives, which is why children in Jakarta and Chicago learn al-Fatiha in the same sounds.

The schools of law hold that a translation can't stand in for the Arabic in the prayer's recitation, though a few early jurists made allowance for someone who couldn't yet manage it; du'a, personal prayer, can be in any language.
It shapes how Muslims read, too. Arabic words often hold several layers at once. Commentators explain rabb, in the Fatiha, as lord, and also the one who raises and nurtures.
English has to choose, and every choice leaves something behind.
So readers often keep a translation open beside the Arabic, and learn a little Arabic even without becoming fluent, to hear what the translation is pointing at.

how: Muslims recite the Qur'an in Arabic in prayer everywhere in the world, and read translations, often printed beside the Arabic, as translations of its meanings rather than as the Qur'an itself.

o: the language Muslims hold the Qur'an came down in
a script kept only for the Qur'an and for prayers
the language most Muslims in the world speak today

they call it a translation of the meanings; the Qur'an is the Arabic.
Pickthall titled his work The Meaning of the Glorious Koran
he wrote that the Qur'an itself can't be translated.
the ritual prayer is said in each person's own language

games.q: a friend holds up an English Qur'an and asks: so this is the Qur'an? what does Pickthall's own title page suggest?
o: it's a translation of its meanings.
games.why: a translation carries the meanings, and it's precious, but Muslims hold the Qur'an itself to be the Arabic.

practice: Say one Arabic word you know softly, bismillah or alhamdulillah, then one English meaning of it, then another, and notice whether either English fills the Arabic. For the last few breaths, let the Arabic sit on its own.
